Robert Louis Stevenson wrote In the South Seas from two Pacific cruises, on the yacht Casco in 1888 and the schooner Equator in 1889. The account covers the Marquesas, the Paumotus, and the Gilbert Islands, where he lived among islanders rather than passing as a tourist. This fine-paper edition appeared in 1908.

Chapters describe landfalls, chiefs and tapus, cannibal valleys, depopulation, traders, and beachcombers, with portraits of particular men and women. The middle sections follow island politics and the movements of elusive traders between atolls. Stevenson mixes travel narrative with early anthropology, asking hard questions about disease, missions, and empire. It remains one of the most thoughtful travel books written about the nineteenth-century Pacific.
